_sources.title: Japan looks to offshore wind to boost energy security, but hurdles remain

1.why: Power measures the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.

2.why: Power is measured in watts (W), where 1 watt equals 1 joule per second.

3.why: Japan has narrow coastal shelves, so floating turbines are needed in deep waters.

wrong.c: Turbines do not stop ocean currents.
wrong.d: Turbines do not heat ocean water.

_quiz_pool.question: What is the formula for power?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Power P equals work W divided by time t.

_quiz_pool.question: If you do the same work in half the time, the power…
_quiz_pool.explanation: Less time means higher power for the same work.

_quiz_pool.question: What is the unit of work W?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Work and energy are measured in joules (J).

_quiz_pool.question: What does energy security mean?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Energy security is having a reliable and secure supply of energy.

_quiz_pool.question: Why are floating wind turbines used in deep water?
options: Fixed towers cannot reach the seabed easily
_quiz_pool.explanation: Deep water makes fixed foundations difficult, so floating platforms anchor to the seabed.

must_show: timing device or observation of speed
_lab_rubric.pass_if: The photos show the paper turbine and hand action, and the student explains how blowing harder changes power.

story.lead: Japan relies on imported fuel for most of its energy [1]. To boost energy security, the country is building offshore wind farms [1].

story.body_1: Japan has a narrow continental shelf, making deep waters common near its coasts [1]. To harness strong sea winds, engineers deploy floating wind turbines that anchor securely to the seabed [1].
story.body_2: While offshore wind offers massive clean power, the sector faces hurdles like high costs, supply chain gaps, and protecting marine fisheries [1]. Weather and climate variability also influence how energy systems operate and plan for the future [2].
timeline.2.text: Commercial floating wind projects launch in Japan [1].
timeline.3.text: Target to reach 30 to 45 GW of offshore wind [1].
physics.title: Work, time and power
physics.body_1: When a wind turbine spins, it does work by transferring energy from moving air to generate electricity. Power measures how fast this energy transfer happens.
physics.body_2: Power is energy divided by time. A higher power means more energy is generated every second.
physics.assumptions: We assume steady wind energy conversion without energy losses in the generator.
table.note: Different energy and time outputs change power.

lab.title: Spinning paper turbine lab
lab.step_1: Cut a paper square and fold diagonals to make a simple pinwheel.
lab.step_2: Blow gently on blades to spin and count rotations in 10 seconds.
lab.step_3: Blow harder to do more work in the same time and observe how speed changes.
lab.question: How does blowing harder change the work and power of your paper turbine?
